meta: Plums from Pomona Britannica, George Brookshaw's 1806 aquatint of fruit grown in the gardens of Hampton Court Palace.
about: Plums fill this plate from Pomona Britannica, a book of fruit grown in the gardens at Hampton Court Palace. Those gardens were the most famous around London. The book set out to show the finest varieties grown in England. George Brookshaw made the plate in 1806, and the Cleveland Museum of Art notes that most of the 90 plates in the large book have dark aquatint backgrounds, as this one does.

meta: Two girls caught mid-dance lesson in Cecilia Beaux's 1898 double portrait Dorothea and Francesca, at the Art Institute of Chicago.
about: Two sisters move together in a dancing lesson. Cecilia Beaux painted them in 1898, and the Art Institute of Chicago says the picture cares more about their matching movement than about who each girl was. They were the daughters of her friends Helena de Kay and Richard Watson Gilder, a well-known couple in New York. The museum reads the scene as a step from girlhood toward adolescence. Beaux won portrait commissions in a market run by men, and she later became the first woman on the faculty of the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts.

meta: Musical instruments in soft window light, with no one to play them: Vilhelm Hammershøi's 1907 Interior. The Music Room, Strandgade 30.
about: Hammershøi lived in a Copenhagen apartment at Strandgade 30 for eleven years and painted its rooms again and again. Here a few musical instruments sit in soft light from a window we can't see. Nobody is playing, and the Art Institute of Chicago says the room feels silent. The museum describes the apartment as a stage set for him, with furniture moved around for how it looked, not how it was used. Rilke wrote that his work is long and slow. Look at the small, flickering brushstrokes.

meta: The racehorse Lexington in a portrait by Thomas J. Scott, who painted him in Kentucky in the 1850s.
about: Lexington was born in Kentucky in 1850 and sired more winning horses than any other American thoroughbred. Thomas J. Scott painted him while living in Kentucky, when the horse was at his peak. Scott also wrote about him for Turf, Field and Farm. He said Lexington was without a peer, very wide across the shoulders and with no surplus ounce on him. The Smithsonian American Art Museum points to the tones in the painting, which bring out the glossy coat and the lean frame.

meta: A huge churning wave on the Maine coast: Winslow Homer's 1887 watercolor Prout's Neck, Breaking Wave.
about: Winslow Homer fished from this spot near Cannon Rock almost every day in summer and fall, so he had watched waves like this a thousand times. That is the account of the Art Institute of Chicago, which cites the scholar Philip Beam. Homer marked out the white foam with resist, probably chalk, then built up the textures of water, rock and sky by layering and scraping the paint. He also blotted and rewetted it. The museum says the picture was carefully planned, though it feels vigorous and immediate.

meta: Golden light over trees and fields in October, John Whetten Ehninger's 1860 harvest landscape at the Smithsonian American Art Museum.
about: Golden light lies over trees and fields, and soft clouds glow above them. John Whetten Ehninger painted the clear air and bright colors of harvest time. The Smithsonian American Art Museum says a scene of peace and plenty hit harder after the Civil War, when it could recall a golden day before cannon fire tore up the fields. The museum quotes a poem from Harper's Weekly that asks what calls back the past like pumpkin pie.

meta: Autumn twilight over a harbor in Siebe Johannes ten Cate's 1901 pastel The Grand Quai of Le Havre, Cleveland Museum of Art.
about: This pastel looks along the quay at Le Havre at dusk in autumn. The Cleveland Museum of Art says it carries the damp chill of that hour. Siebe Johannes ten Cate was born in Holland. Most of his career was in Paris. For a short time he shared a Montmartre apartment with Kees van Dongen, and he knew Vincent van Gogh too. He was known for harbors and cityscapes. Here the light is nearly gone.

meta: A snake crawling over memorial offerings in Hokusai's Memorial Anniversary, a print from One Hundred Ghost Tales, 1831 to 1832.
about: A snake slides over the things set out for a memorial service: a box of sweets, a spirit tablet with the dead person's Buddhist name, and a green leaf floating in a bowl of water. The snake stands for malice. Hokusai seems to have planned a hundred prints, but only five are known. The title comes from a game where people told scary stories at night and snuffed a candle after each one. The Art Institute of Chicago adds that the bright blue was new and cheap, though viewers then linked it with death.

meta: Whistler holding his palette in front of Japanese scrolls and Chinese porcelain in The Artist in His Studio, 1865 to 1866.
about: Whistler looks straight out at us with a palette and brush in hand. Behind him hang three Japanese scrolls, and Chinese porcelain sits on shelves to the left. He used thin layers of muted paint so the surface would look as flat as a Japanese woodblock print. The Art Institute of Chicago also sees Velázquez here, since Las Meninas has a painter who shows himself at his easel as well. Whistler, an American living in London, put himself at the center of that mix of East and West.

meta: Mount Fuji reflected in the still surface of Lake Misaka in Hokusai's 1832 color woodcut, held by the Library of Congress.
about: The still surface of Lake Misaka acts like a mirror, and Mount Fuji hangs upside down in it. Hokusai made this color woodcut in 1832. The Library of Congress describes it as a print of the lake's mirror surface with the reflection of the mountain. Look at where the real shoreline ends and the reflection begins.

meta: A merchant family in Turkish and European dress on a yellow divan in Izmir: Antoine de Favray's 1769 portrait of the Van Lennep family.
about: David George van Lennep, chief merchant of the Dutch trading post at Smyrna, sits on a long yellow divan with his wife Anna Maria and their youngest son on her lap. She wears Turkish dress and he wears European clothes and holds two letters. Her father sits beside them with a moustache, and the children's tutor leafs through a book. The two eldest sons stand at the front, one with a sword and the other with a violin and bow. Antoine de Favray painted the family in 1769.

meta: A rider passes a beggar with an outstretched arm on a country road in Jan Wijnants's hilly landscape, painted in 1655.
about: A rider trots along a country road through hilly ground and passes a beggar who holds out his arm. In the distance there are trees and a ridge of hills. The Rijksmuseum's description stops there. It doesn't say who the rider is or why the scene was painted. Jan Wijnants painted it in 1655.

meta: The Court of Holland around 1610 with a beheading on the Green Sod, a print by Bartholomeus Willemsz. Dolendo from Orlers's history of Maurice of Nassau.
about: A beheading takes place on the Green Sod while a crowd gathers to watch. On the right are the Prisoner's Gate, the buildings of the Binnenhof and the Court Pond, and on the left the Buitenhof. This is the Court of Holland in The Hague around 1610. The print was made for Jan Orlers's account of the victories won under Prince Maurice of Nassau, first published at Leiden in 1610. The same plate appeared again in the French edition of 1612.

meta: Three scenes under the motto Unity makes strength mark the 1872 celebration of the capture of Den Briel, a print by Amand held by the Rijksmuseum.
about: The print marks the national celebration of 1 April 1872, three hundred years after the Sea Beggars took Den Briel. Three scenes run across the sheet under the motto Unity makes strength. On the left, three Dutchmen break the Spanish yoke in 1572. In the middle, Freedom takes the hand of the Dutch Maiden in 1872. On the right is a house in 1800 hung with ribbons and slogans. Flowers and flags surround all three. The scenes decorated the house of Remmert de Vries in Zaandam, and a printed explanation went with the sheet.

meta: Berthe Morisot printed her drypoint of herself with her daughter Julie Manet in 1888, and later editions followed in 1904, 1921 and about 1930.
about: Morisot and her daughter Julie Manet share this print, known as The Drawing Lesson. Her prints were first pulled between 1888 and 1890. Ernst Rouart reissued them as a series in 1904 and 1905. A second reissue came in 1921. The last one, around 1930, was made by the publisher Vollard and the printer Fort, and Vollard then cancelled the series by punching holes at the top and bottom of each plate. The British Museum holds another impression.

meta: The devil in disguise asks a woman with a child to follow him in Jean Baptiste Madou's 1829 print for a Belgian book of old court cases.
about: A disguised devil asks a woman carrying a child to go with him. Jean Baptiste Madou made the print for a book about old Belgian criminal law, told through unusual verdicts from earlier times. Joseph Bernaert Cannaert wrote it, and it came out in Brussels in 1829 from the publisher Brest van Kempen.

meta: The centaur Nessus carries off Dejanira while Hercules aims from the rocks: Gustave Moreau's painting of about 1872, also called Autumn.
about: The centaur Nessus offered to carry Dejanira across a river. Now he is carrying her off. Her husband Hercules has already crossed and hides in the rocks ahead, with a poisoned arrow ready to fly. Gustave Moreau paints the centaur dark and muscular and Dejanira pale and slim. The Getty says the pair look more like dancers than people in a struggle. Moreau meant the picture to join a set about the seasons, which is why it is also called Autumn.

meta: A laughing woman points at a medallion with a nude on it in Gerard van Honthorst's 1625 painting at the Saint Louis Art Museum.
about: A laughing woman in gold and red points at a small medallion she holds up. It shows a seated nude hiding her face behind a hand, with a Dutch caption asking who could recognize her from behind. Wikipedia reads the woman as a prostitute advertising her services, a common practice in the Netherlands during the Eighty Years' War. Gerard van Honthorst painted her in 1625, and the same sitter probably appears in his De koppelaarster from that year. The painter's name was forgotten until 1922.

meta: Moses and Aaron watch the Israelites gather falling quails in Jacopo Bassano's 1554 painting, made for the Venetian Domenico Priuli.
about: Moses and Aaron stand on the left with their heads bowed in talk. The rest of the canvas is full of Israelites gathering quails that fall from the sky. The Venetian nobleman Domenico Priuli ordered the picture in 1554, and Jacopo Bassano's account book records the payments. The subject is rare in painting. The Getty says the hills behind the tents recall the pre-Alps near Bassano, the painter's hometown.

meta: Sarah Bernhardt posed as Mary Magdalene with a skull and long hair in Alfred Stevens's 1887 painting, now in Ghent.
about: Sarah Bernhardt posed for this Mary Magdalene. Alfred Stevens met the actress around 1887 and painted her several times in historical and literary roles. Here she has long hair and a skull, and a bare landscape stretches behind her. Wikipedia says her sad, sensual gaze at the viewer blurs the religious subject, and that the picture shocked a public who wanted a repentant Magdalene. The Paris merchant Georges Petit ordered it. The Museum of Fine Arts in Ghent has had it since 2001.

meta: Govert Flinck's 1638 Landscape with an Obelisk was stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston in 1990 and has not been found.
about: Thieves took this landscape from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston on 18 March 1990, and nobody has seen it since. Govert Flinck painted it in 1638 on a wood panel a little over two feet wide. It was once thought to be by Rembrandt. A reward of 10 million dollars is still offered for the return of the stolen works.

meta: Judith and her maid Abra hold Holofernes down in Artemisia Gentileschi's Uffizi painting of about 1620.
about: Judith and her maid Abra pin Holofernes down and cut off his head. Their sleeves are rolled up as if this were a household chore, and Judith drives the sword straight down while blood arcs across the scene. Holofernes pushes against the maid and cannot get free. Artemisia Gentileschi painted this version around 1620, and it hangs in the Uffizi in Florence. Wikipedia says it improves on her earlier version from about 1612, now in Naples, in its composition and detail.

meta: Grapes, apples, pears and an open pomegranate with tiny insects and snails: Luca Forte's still life on copper from the 1630s.
about: Grapes, apples and pears sit beside an open pomegranate full of seeds, and tiny insects and snails crawl over the fruit. The Getty says the original meaning is lost, but it may refer to the abundance of autumn. Luca Forte painted it in the 1630s on a small copper panel, which gives the surface a smooth, enamel-like finish. The museum adds that Forte brought landscape backgrounds into Neapolitan still life, in place of the plain dark ground used before him.

meta: Fashionable Victorians play lawn tennis in John Lavery's 1885 painting, which won a gold medal at the Paris Salon of 1888.
about: Fashionable Victorians play lawn tennis in this painting by John Lavery, one of the Glasgow Boys. The sport was brand new. The first Wimbledon Championship had been held only a few years before. Lavery painted the scene in 1885 and showed it at the Royal Academy that year. It won a gold medal at the Paris Salon of 1888, which Wikipedia calls his breakthrough. James Murray gave it to Aberdeen Art Gallery in 1926.

meta: A blue stream runs from a cave mouth in Gustave Courbet's Grotto of Sarrazine, painted about 1864 with palette knives.
about: A clear blue stream runs out of a tunnel-like cave in the Jura Mountains, Courbet's home region in eastern France, and two large boulders stand in front of it. Gustave Courbet scraped and spread the paint with palette knives and worked brushes into wet paint to copy the rough, colored rock. The Getty thinks he was probably drawn to the grotto for its geology, like many visitors of his day. He painted caves often in the mid 1860s.

meta: Nicolaes Maes copied Albrecht Durer's Nativity engraving and added four shepherds in this painting of about 1660.
about: Nicolaes Maes copied Albrecht Dürer's 1504 engraving of the Nativity almost exactly. He widened the house on the left, gave the Virgin and the child new poses, and added four shepherds, which gave the picture its new subject. The blacks, browns and whites he chose keep the look of a print, and the oil paint lets him render the wooden door, the bare bricks and the thatched roof. The Getty dates it to about 1660.

meta: A young man lies stretched out with a lute in François Boucher's 1736 chalk drawing on blue paper.
about: A young man lies stretched out on a heap of fabric, plucking a lute or a similar instrument. His back is to us and his face is half hidden, so the twist of his body is what holds the eye. François Boucher drew him in 1736 in black, red and white chalk on blue paper, a technique called aux trois crayons. The Getty says it is one of very few surviving drawings for his first set of designs for woven wall hangings, the Fêtes italiennes.

meta: Flora, goddess of spring, sits in a grotto holding jasmine and columbine in Francesco Melzi's painting of about 1520.
about: Flora, the Roman goddess of spring and flowers, sits in a grotto among ferns and ivy. She wears a white gown embroidered in gold with a blue cloak over one shoulder, holds jasmine in her lap and a spray of columbine in her left hand. The columbine gave the painting its old name, La Columbina. Francesco Melzi painted it about 1520 in the manner of Leonardo, whose face type and soft shading he follows. Marie de' Medici owned it in 1649, and the Hermitage has had it since 1850.

meta: Paolo Veronese's Wedding at Cana, ordered by Benedictine monks in Venice in 1562, is the largest painting in the Louvre.
about: Veronese's Wedding at Cana is the largest picture in the Louvre, nearly ten metres wide. Benedictine monks on the island of San Giorgio in Venice ordered it for their new dining hall in 1562. Their contract paid Veronese 324 ducats, a barrel of wine and his meals, and asked for the best colors, ultramarine above all. He delivered it in 1563. Soldiers of Napoleon's army took the canvas as war booty in 1797.
